items.excerpt: Google has unveiled Expert Intelligence, a new initiative enabling readers to access purchased e-books and other trusted sources within its AI products, incorporating over 100,000 publisher titles.
Google unveiled Expert Intelligence, an AI feature letting readers interact with e-books through questions, quizzes, and infographics while publishers praised its copyright safeguards.
David Crotty lays out The Scholarly Kitchen's policy on AI use, clarifying that AI cannot author posts or generate images, but transparent AI-assisted editing and drafting is permitted.

Todd Carpenter examines Anthropic's new watermarking system for AI-generated content, arguing it addresses regulatory compliance but not the deeper problem of attribution and provenance in publishing.
Avi Staiman and Hong Zhou explore how AI research assistants that learn user preferences risk becoming intellectual echo chambers that mirror assumptions rather than challenge them.

Tim O'Reilly argues AI should be treated as a creative medium rather than a threat to authorship, revealing in the afterword of an essay that 'Claude wrote every word' while he directed the collaboration.
A new typeface called Decoy Font uses layered letterforms with clear outlines over blurred shapes so humans can read the text but large language models cannot parse it.

Author Kyla Zhao examines how algorithmic curation threatens creative taste and advocates for intentional 'wandering' to preserve authentic aesthetic choices against predictable, AI-driven consumption patterns.
Tracy Cooper-Posey discusses forming a personal AI-use policy to cut decision fatigue, sharing how a clear framework let her stop relitigating AI questions in her author business every day.
